questions.question: What informal idea does continuity express?
options: Every function has a sudden jump.
Small input changes lead to small output changes.
Only finite sets can be used as domains.
The output is the same for every input.
questions.explanation: Continuity expresses local stability: by restricting $x$ sufficiently close to $x_0$, the output can be forced arbitrarily close to $f(x_0)$.
questions.source_support: Interpretation of continuity.

option_explanations: A jump is a standard failure of continuity, not its defining feature.
Continuity is defined on intervals and many infinite domains.
Equal outputs for every input define a constant function, only one continuous example.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.explanation: Continuity on a set is pointwise: the continuity condition must hold at each $x_0\in X$.

The function value may be nonzero; the condition compares nearby outputs with it.
Continuity controls all sufficiently close $x$, not only the centre.

questions.question: Continuity of $f$ at $x_0$ is equivalent to which limit statement?
questions.explanation: Continuity at $x_0$ is exactly existence of the limit together with equality to the actual value $f(x_0)$.

option_explanations: The limit must equal the actual value $f(x_0)$, not $0$; e.g. for $f(x)=x^2$ at $x_0=2$, continuity requires $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=4=f(2)$, and $4\ne0$.
A limit unequal to $f(x_0)$ gives a removable discontinuity.
A zero centre value alone gives no information about nearby outputs.

questions.question: Is a constant function $f(x)=c$ continuous on $\mathbb{R}$?
options: Yes; it is continuous at every real input
No; it has a jump at every real input
Yes; but only at the input $x=0$
Yes; but only when its value $c=0$
questions.explanation: For a constant function, $|f(x)-f(x_0)|=|c-c|=0$ for every $x$, so every tolerance is met.
questions.source_support: Small input changes give small (here zero) output changes.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Constants have identical left and right values, hence no jumps.
The same zero output difference holds at every real $x_0$, not only zero.
The proof uses $c-c=0$ for any real $c$.

questions.question: If $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $x_0$, what can be concluded about $f+g$ at $x_0$?
questions.explanation: The sum law gives $\lim(f+g)=\lim f+\lim g=f(x_0)+g(x_0)=(f+g)(x_0)$.
